title: Merging pairs
objectives: Write the byte-pair encoding training loop and run its first merges by hand.

screens.title: Count again after a merge
screens.prose: After merge 1, every `b i` is the new token `bi`, id 256. The counts must be taken on this new row, not on the bytes. That loop of count, merge, count is **byte-pair encoding** (BPE).
screens.question: Count each pair in the new row.

hints.text: Read pairs off the new row of 19 cells.
Every `i` that was followed by `d` is now inside `bi`.
`bi d` 4 times, space `bi` 3 times, `i d` no longer anywhere.

feedback.correct: 4, 3 and 0. The next merge is `bi` with `d`, the token `bid`.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count on the row as it is after the merge.

byKey.old-bytes: You counted on the original bytes. After the merge each of those `i`s sits inside `bi`, so `i d` is gone.
byKey.with-start: The first `bi` starts the text, so no space comes before it: 3, not 4.

explain.text: Counts always come from the current row. `i d` was 4 on the bytes, but merge 1 swallowed every one of those `i`s. Next `bi d` wins with 4.

screens.title: Overlapping pairs
screens.prose: Our rule counts every position where a pair starts, so pairs may overlap. A position size in an order log reads `1000`.
screens.question: Under our rule, how many times does the pair `0` then `0` occur in `1000`?

hints.text: List the starting positions of every pair of neighbours.
Positions 1 to 2 and 2 to 3 both hold `0 0`.
Two positions start the pair, so the count is 2.

feedback.correct: Two: positions 1 and 2 both start the pair `0 0`.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count positions, letting pairs share a byte.

byKey.no-overlap: You counted without overlaps, as if each byte could join only one pair. Our counting rule lets the middle 0 belong to both.
byKey.zeros: That is the number of zeros. Three zeros make two neighbouring pairs.

explain.text: The count is 2, yet the merge itself runs left to right and replaces only one, giving `1`, `00`, `0`. Counting and merging are different steps; state the counting rule, because another rule gives another tokeniser.

screens.title: Breaking a tie
screens.prose: In `papa mama`, `pa` and `ma` each appear twice. Our rule: on a tie, merge the pair that occurs first in the sequence.
screens.question: Which pair does our rule merge first?

options.why: You broke the tie alphabetically. Our rule takes the pair that occurs first in the text.
`ap` occurs once, between the two `pa`s. It is not in the tie.
One merge makes one new id. The other pair can win a later round.

hints.text: Both have count 2.
Which of them appears first, reading from the left?
`pa` starts at position 0; `ma` first starts at position 5.

feedback.correct: `pa`: it appears first in the sequence.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply the tie rule: the pair that occurs first.

byKey.ma: Alphabetical order is another valid rule, and it gives another tokeniser. Ours takes the earliest pair.

explain.text: `pa` occurs first, so it becomes id 256. A different tie rule gives a different, equally valid tokeniser: the merge list must record which pairs were chosen.

screens.title: The training loop
screens.prose:
Here is what you did, as code. New ids run from 256, and the loop stops when no pair appears twice.
```python
ids = list(text.encode('utf-8'))
merges = []
for k in range(n_merges):
    counts = pair_counts(ids)
    if not counts:
        break
    pair = max(counts, key=counts.get)
    if counts[pair] < 2:
        break
    ids = merge(ids, pair, 256 + k)
    merges.append(pair)
```
screens.question: Why does `max(counts, key=counts.get)` follow our tie rule?

options.text: Keys keep first-seen order; `max` keeps the first maximum
`max` sorts the pairs and returns the smallest on a tie
options.why: `max` does not sort; on a tie it keeps the first key it met.

options.text: Ties are rare, so any choice will do
options.why: Ties are common, as `bi` and `id` showed. The rule must be fixed to repeat a tokeniser.

options.text: `max` returns the last of equal values, the newest pair
options.why: It returns the first one it meets, the pair seen earliest.

hints.text: In what order does `pair_counts` add keys to the dict?

feedback.correct: Keys enter the dict in the order pairs first occur, and `max` keeps the first maximum.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about the dict's key order and what `max` does on a tie.

explain.text: `pair_counts` adds each pair when first seen, so key order is sequence order. `max` returns the first key with the largest count, which is our tie rule.

mutants.source:
def pair_counts(ids):
    counts, i = {}, 0
    while i + 1 < len(ids):
        p = (ids[i], ids[i + 1])
        counts[p] = counts.get(p, 0) + 1
        i += 2 if ids[i] == ids[i + 1] else 1
    return counts
mutants.symptom: Skips a byte after a repeated pair, so overlaps such as aaa count once.
Sorts the pairs, so the first-seen order the tie rule needs is lost.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 is `[97, 97, 97]`, which holds the pair twice. Count every position; do not skip a byte after a match.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 checks the key order. Add pairs as you meet them, left to right, so ties break the same way.

explain.text: `zip(ids, ids[1:])` walks every position once, so overlaps count. A plain dict keeps first-seen order, which the tie rule needs.

mutants.source:
def train_bpe(text, n_merges):
    ids = list(text.encode('utf-8'))
    merges = []
    for k in range(n_merges):
        counts = pair_counts(ids)
        if not counts:
            break
        pair = max(counts, key=counts.get)
        ids = merge(ids, pair, 256 + k)
        merges.append(pair)
    return merges

Counts every round on the original bytes instead of the current ids.

screens.title: Compressing an order log
screens.prose: A desk keeps a log of order messages. Trained on it, BPE's first eight merges are listed below; they take the 63-byte log to 35 tokens.
screens.question: What do the first merges of an order log capture?

options.text: Fields that recur on many lines: NEW, BUY, 00
The prices, because numbers merge first
options.why: Numbers merge only where they repeat: the round sizes 100 and 200 share `00`. A varied price would not.

options.text: The rarest tickers, to save space on them
options.why: BPE always merges the most frequent pair; a rare ticker stays as bytes longest.

options.text: Nothing useful: BPE is built for English
options.why: It works on any bytes. A log's repeated fields compress well.

hints.text: BPE merges the most frequent pair.
Which strings appear on almost every line?
`NEW`, ` BUY` and `00` recur; tickers and sizes vary more.

feedback.correct: The recurring fields come first, so a log's boilerplate costs few tokens.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about which pairs are most frequent in the log.

explain.text: The most frequent pairs come from text repeated on many lines: the field names and the round sizes. Fields that vary, such as unusual prices, stay as several tokens.

ideas: Byte-pair encoding starts from bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent pair of neighbours into a new id, 256 upwards.
Count on the current ids, overlaps included; merge left to right; on a tie take the pair that occurs first; stop when no pair appears twice.
More merges mean shorter sequences and a larger embedding table; each merge saves less than the one before.
